chapter_theme: The limits of tapas (தவ நிந்தை): once the Life of life is within and samadhi is in hand, recitation, chant, purity rites and even tapas fall away; true tapas is knowing the outcome, cutting the senses with the sword of understanding, a single-pointed mind and the fellowship of those already in Siva's bliss. Those without tapas or learning only whirl around for food.
structure_note: The title, literally 'reproach of tapas', is not borne out as an attack: the verses list what becomes needless (1633, 1634, 1644), redefine true tapas (1635, 1638, 1639, 1641) and fault those with none (1642).

1633.reading: Recitation is not needed if the Life of life has come within; desire is not needed if one sees the true body as its place; dying is not needed if samadhi is in hand; going about is not needed for those who do not follow the senses.
1633.nuance: Each line pairs a practice or urge with the attainment that makes it needless. மெய்க்காயம் இடம் கண்டால் may mean seeing the body as the Lord's dwelling, in line with Tirumular's body-as-temple teaching. சாதலும் வேண்டாம் may be that death is overcome or that one need not seek death; போதல் may be pilgrimage.

1634.reading: No need to cry out once one has grasped the meaning and grown calm; no need of sounded chant once samadhi is in hand; no need of purification for one who stands free of pollution; no need even of the mind for one who rests without action.
1634.nuance: சத்தம் may be audible chant or sound in general. துடக்கு is ritual pollution (as from birth or death) and also attachment, so line 3 can be ritual or moral. The last line goes furthest: the mind itself is put among the things that become needless.

1635.reading: Those who know the outcome do the true tapas of old, speak the true word of old and do the true dharma of old; those who know the outcome surpass those of heaven and of earth.
1635.nuance: விளைவு, what grows from an act, is the fruit of deeds; to know it is to see where each act leads. பண்டை, of old, presents the right way as ancient rather than new.

1636.reading: Doing tapas in company, I saw the sounding anklets; doing tapas in search, I saw the Siva-state; is wasting oneself away tapas? If they cast these off and quarrel, what tapas have the many worldly people?
1636.nuance: Line 3 (வாடித் தவஞ்செய்வதே தவம்) can be read as a statement, 'tapas done in wasting is tapas', or as a question, which fits the chapter's criticism of mortification. கூடி may be 'in the company of devotees' or 'united with the Lord'. Line 4 is obscure.

1637.reading: Those who have swum with their arms across the seven great seas of the mind come into the shelter of the people of tapas; if those still in the round of birth listen to them and serve them, they may come face to face with Nandi.
1637.nuance: The seven seas are not explained; they may be the mind's restless states, seven births or the seven bodily centres. The verse gives a chain of mediation: the tapasvins reach shelter, and the worldly reach Nandi through serving them.

1638.reading: Draw the sword of understanding that stands in the mind, cut yourself from the crowd, cleave it so that no two remain, and turn back the five so they do not stray into the field: then, within tapas, the light of the way becomes your own light.
1638.nuance: புனம், the millet field, is the field of sense objects and the five are the senses, as tradition reads them. இனம் may be the senses as a band or bad company. ஆறொளி may be the light of the path or the light of the six centres; the plain sense is that discipline makes the light one's own.

1639.reading: To speak of him who stands equal to all and beyond all gives devotion; the sage gives release to the devotees who bow and worship; to act in that state as one who is real is itself tapas.
1639.nuance: ஒத்து மிகவும் நின்றான், one who is equal and also exceeds, is taken as the Lord who is in all and beyond all. சத்தான செய்வது (doing what is sat, real) is the verse's definition of tapas, but its sense is not fixed: it may be acting as the real self, or doing what is true.

1640.reading: Touching leaves and plucking flowers, I gathered them thinking 'for my father', but did not see the water that comes; seeing the scripture that reaches the summit my heart bowed, and touching the summit I saw how tapas is taken up.
1640.nuance: The verse moves from outer worship (leaves, flowers, water for the Lord's bath) to something reached at the தலை, head or summit. தலை தொட்ட நூல் may be the highest scripture, and தலை தொட்டு may be touching one's head in reverence or, yogically, reaching the crown. வரும் புனல் காணேன் may be a confession of incomplete outer worship or a hint at inner water.

1641.reading: The Lord grants that no trouble reaches the devotees who hold to the great tapas of matted hair; looked at truly, the tapas of those who take on hardship lies in a single mind that holds the body in check.
1641.nuance: Line 3 (இடரடை செய்தவர்) can be those who take on hardship or those who cause it; line 4's உடரடை is read as உடல் அடை, holding the body. The verse seems to move the worth of tapas from outward marks to one-pointedness of mind.

1642.reading: Like one who, frightened by a crocodile lying in the river, runs off and meets a she-bear that has just given birth, so are those who do no tapas and do not know the books, standing and whirling around for rice.
1642.nuance: ஈற்றுக் கரடி, a bear that has just whelped, is at its fiercest; fleeing one danger, the man meets a worse. The verse's target is a life spent chasing food, where each escape leads to a new danger.

1643.reading: Those who can tie up in its stall the frisking young calf that keeps butting at the sack will find in the heart, without slipping, how the fruit ripens and how the fruit is eaten.
1643.nuance: The calf is traditionally the mind and the stall the place it is held; கோணி may be a sack of fodder or something bent. The ripening and eating of the fruit is the fruit of discipline coming to fulfilment, but the verse does not name the fruit.

1644.reading: No tapas is needed to make the mind Siva if one has kinship with those whose minds have joined Siva's bliss; when the mind becomes Siva, siddhi and release follow; the mind becoming Siva is the fruit of tapas done.
1644.nuance: The verse gives two routes to one end: fellowship (உறவு) with those in Siva's bliss, which makes tapas unnecessary, and tapas itself, whose fruit is the same. Sengalvaraya notes a parallel in Tiruvasagam (அச்சோப் பதிகம் 1), where the Lord removes the mind's malas and makes it Siva.

links.note: 1632 says tapas falls away once the samadhi of knowledge is reached; 1644 adds a second way past it, fellowship with those already in Siva's bliss, and names the end both serve: the mind becoming Siva.
Both tie want to the lack of tapas: the Kural says the poor are many because few practise austerity, Tirumular pictures those without tapas or learning whirling around for rice.
Both picture those who do no tapas as shut out and reduced to want: in the Naladiyar they cling to the outer door of others' houses, in Tirumular they run from crocodile to bear in search of rice.

The Kural asks for flawless learning followed by living by it; Tirumular says recitation (ஓதல்) is no longer needed once the Life of life is within. The two speak of different stages, so this limits learning rather than contradicting it.

1633 says that once samadhi is in hand dying is not needed (சாதலும் வேண்டாம் சமாதிகை கூடினால்). 2320 opens with the same condition, the samadhi where oneself becomes Him (சமாதிகை கூடினால்), and says malam is cut and the flawless body stays on the earth (ஈனமில் காயம் இருக்கும் இருநிலத்து). Read together, 2320 spells out what 1633's 'no need to die' means: the body itself remains, freed of defect.

A near-repeat: both verses run the same frame, X வேண்டாம் once a state is reached, and both name samadhi in hand (சமாதிகை கூடினால்) as the state that makes outward practice needless. 1633 sets aside recitation, desire and wandering; 1634 sets aside crying out, chant, purification and finally the mind itself (சித்தமும் வேண்டாம்), so the pair shows how far the list is pushed.

1635 says those who know the outcome (விளைவறிவார்) do the true tapas of old and surpass those of heaven and earth. Kural 266 says those who do tapas do their own work (தங்கருமம் செய்வார்) and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile. Both treat tapas as the act of one who sees where deeds lead, the Kural naming the failure as அவம் and Tirumular the insight as விளைவு.

1636 says 'seeking, doing tapas, I saw the Siva-state' and 'joining, I saw the sounding anklets' (தேடித் ... கூடி ... குரைகழல்). 1654 runs the same verbs as a chain, தேடுவன் தேடி, கூடுவன் கூடிக் குரைகழற்கே, and ends in not letting go until release. The shared seeking-joining-anklets sequence, outside 1636's doubts about wasting the body, is the positive path both verses point to.

1637 says the worldly who listen to and serve the people of tapas (பணி கேட்கின்) may come face to face with Nandi. Kural 443 says the rarest of rare things is to cherish the great and make them one's own (பெரியாரைப் பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்). Tirumular carries the Kural's counsel on choosing great companions into the spiritual sphere, where service of the tapasvins becomes the way to the Lord.

1638 says to turn back the five so they do not stray into the field (புனத்திடை அஞ்சும் போகாமல் மறித்தால்), and then the light of the way becomes one's own. Kural 343 says the field of the five must be crushed (அடல்வேண்டும் ஐந்தன் புலத்தை) and all desires let go together. Both locate discipline in checking the five senses at their field; Tirumular adds the sword of understanding and the inner light that follows.

1639 says the sage gives release to devotees who bow and worship (பணிந்தடி யார்தொழ முத்தி கொடுக்கும்). 284 has the same words, பணிந்தடி யார்தொழ முத்தி கொடுத்தவர், and adds that even siddhas cannot discern him otherwise. The repeated formula shows Tirumular naming bowed worship, not knowledge or powers, as what the Lord answers with release.

1640 tells of gathering leaves and flowers 'for my father' yet not seeing the water that comes (வரும்புனல் காணேன்), and finding tapas only on reaching the summit. 1828 says for those who do good there are flowers and water (பூவுண்டு நீருண்டு) and the Lord sees and grants grace. 1640 limits 1828's plain assurance: flowers gathered in outer worship are a start, but the speaker found tapas only beyond them.

Kural 261 defines tapas as bearing the pain that comes and causing no pain to others (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்). 1641 says that, truly seen, the tapas of those who take on hardship (இடரடை செய்தவர்) lies in a single mind holding the body (ஒருமனத் தாமே). Tirumular keeps the Kural's endurance but adds the condition that it counts as tapas only when the mind is one-pointed.

1643 says those who can tie the frisking calf in its stall (குழக்கன்று கொட்டிலிற் கட்டவல்லார்) will find the fruit ripening in the heart. 2024 says a beast will not keep to the road even when a learned mahout climbs on its neck and goads it (அம்மா வழிநடவாதே). Both picture the mind as an unruly animal; 2024 limits 1643's promise by stressing how rarely learning and force alone make it obey.

Kural 265 says tapas is striven for here because what is wanted is gained as it is wanted (வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங் கெய்தலால் செய்தவம்). 1644 agrees that the fruit of tapas (செய்தவப் பேறு) is the mind becoming Siva, but says tapas is not needed (செய்தவம் வேண்டா) for one who has kinship with those already in Siva's bliss. It adds a second route to the fruit the Kural ties to tapas alone.

source_issues: 1636 line 4 (இவைகளைந் தூடிற் பலவுல கோரெத் தவரே) and 1643 lines 2-3 (கோணியைப் பல்காற் குழக்கன்று) are obscure and may be corrupt.
